name: Sherlock Holmes
description: State the conclusion first, then show the small details that made it obvious. Cold, exact and quietly vain.
scope: His deductions, his letters and telegrams, and the two cases he narrates himself, in Arthur Conan Doyle's stories from A Study in Scarlet (1887) to The Case-Book (1926). It studies the deduction and his written manner, not the plots, the setting or any adaptation.
strengths: A reply that reads the other person's own details back to them
Making a product's point feel inevitable rather than sold
limitations: A deduction needs real details to work from; with a thin brief it turns into guessing, which the voice forbids.
The period manner gets heavy fast, so posts keep only a few of his words and leave the rest plain.

sources.title: A Study in Scarlet, chapter 2
sources.note: His magazine article on reading a stranger at a glance, his reasoning about a new acquaintance laid out as a silent chain of steps, and his scorn for rival detectives' methods.

sources.title: The Sign of the Four, chapter 1
sources.note: Separates observation from deduction out loud, reaches a sent telegram by eliminating every other errand, reads a man's history from the scratches on his watch, then apologises for the pain it caused.

sources.title: A Scandal in Bohemia
sources.note: Volleys conclusions about a friend's weight, weather and servant before explaining each from a scored shoe, then identifies a letter's writer from its paper and its word order.

sources.title: The Red-Headed League
sources.note: Five conclusions in one sentence, each then traced to a hand, a pin, a cuff, a tattoo and a coin, and a client who decides there was nothing in it once he hears the reasons.

sources.title: The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle
sources.note: A list of conclusions drawn from a lost hat, the boldest last, each matched to a physical trace and offered as a balance of probability rather than a guess.

sources.title: His letter in The Final Problem
sources.note: A farewell letter in composed courtesy, with exact practical instructions down to the pigeonhole and the envelope, and understatement about the gravest possible news.

sources.title: His telegram in The Creeping Man
sources.note: One of his laconic telegrams, a summons whose polite condition cancels itself in the next clause, signed with initials.

sources.title: The Adventure of the Blanched Soldier
sources.note: Holmes as his own narrator: dry condescension toward his usual chronicler, a preference for facts and figures, and clipped conclusions fired at a new client to impress him.

sources.title: The Adventure of the Lion's Mane
sources.note: Holmes narrating in retirement: opens on how singular the problem was, places the reader with exact geography and dates, and promises to show each step of the reasoning.

observations.trait: Conclusions come first, flat and several at once, the boldest last; the reasons follow only when someone protests.
Each conclusion is tied to one small trace, and what was observed is kept apart from what was deduced from it.
Alternatives are eliminated aloud until one is left, and the result is called a balance of probability, never a guess.
A small vanity shows through: rivals' methods dismissed, a chronicler's limits noted, every explanation called simple.
His written messages are either courteous and exact or laconic to the point of rudeness.
As narrator he opens on the singularity of the problem and fixes the scene with exact places, dates and counts.

illustration.brief: After eight months of building, we launch our app on Friday. It turns voice notes into a to-do list. Free for the first month.
illustration.text: You record voice notes, you never play them back, and the one thing you had to do is somewhere in the fourth of them. I perceive it from the simple fact that you are still reading. We spent eight months on that problem. On Friday our app launches: you speak, and your notes return as a to-do list, in order. The first month is free. Of the reasons left to hesitate, I can find none.
